newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli PM takes tough stance on occupied Arab land.
newsitem.headline: Israeli PM takes tough stance on occupied Arab land.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took a hard line on peace talks with both Syria and the Palestinians, ruling out a return of the occupied land they want back.

"No one should think for an instant that I changed any stance to which I am committed," Netanyahu said in remarks to Israeli reporters in the United States on Friday that were broadcast in Israel on Saturday.
Netanyahu said Palestinians would not receive most of the occupied West Bank as they expected and it was up to Damascus to resume peace talks with Israel.

"This government is not galloping towards the 1967 lines and we will not return to the 1967 lines," he told army radio, referring to Israel's borders before it occupied the West Bank, Gaza Strip and Golan Heights.
Netanyahu, on a visit to the United States to discuss Middle East peace, told Israel radio it was up to Syrian President Hafez al-Assad to decide if talks between the arch-foes resume.
"President Assad rules in Syria...there is no real excuse for Syria not to enter peace talks with Israel. If he wants to, he can. If he can't, it means he doesn't want to," he said.

Asked if Assad wanted to resume the talks broken off by Israel a year ago, Netanyahu said: "Why should I estimate? In a short time we'll know if there's a Syrian response to American efforts to restart the negotiations."
Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara and Vice-President Abdel-Halim Khaddam were in Cairo on Saturday to discuss Middle East peace with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.

"The Israeli government is the one running away from peace and not the Syrian leadership. Syria is ready to resume negotiations tomorrow if Israel abides by what was reached during the previous stage," Shara said.

Israel and Syria failed in sporadic talks from 1991 to agree on the Golan. Syria insists on the return of all the strategic plateau. Israel's previous government said it was willing to make at least a partial pullback but Netanyahu has insisted on keeping all the territory.
Syria wants talks to resume from where they left off a year ago. Netanyahu said on Friday he would "take note" of anything agreed in earlier talks but stressed he was not committed to it.
Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said on Friday Netanyahu had brought to Washington a "creative" formula to reopen talks with Syria but declined to elaborate.
Netanyahu also rejected Palestinian territorial hopes, insisting the PLO would not get most of the West Bank and Gaza in "final status" peace talks due to commence in March.

"The Palestinians will not receive most of the territory as they are saying. We oppose the creation of a (Palestinian) state and of course we staunchly oppose any harm to our sovereignty in Jerusalem."

The Palestine Liberation Organisation, which wants to establish an independent Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza with Arab East Jerusalem as its capital, expected to receive most of the occupied land in a final settlement.

Netanyahu said a final accord with the PLO must guarantee Israel can defend itself from "possible terrorist attacks" from PLO-run areas and from the "possible creation of an eastern front" against Israel.
Israel and the PLO were to resume talks on Sunday on implementing outstanding issues in interim peace deals.
